UX Research Study

Why do young adults struggle to track their money?

Most people in their late teens and twenties want to manage their money better — yet the tools built for that job go unused within weeks. This is a look at why, built from survey data, interviews, secondary research, and a close read of the tools already on the market.

AudienceStudents & early professionals, 18–25
MethodSurvey, interviews, secondary research, landscape review
My roleResearch & synthesis, part of a 3-person team
01
Context

Money management is a habit no one taught this generation.

Budgeting and expense-tracking apps promise to make money simple: log what comes in, log what goes out, and let the app do the thinking. In practice, most of the people they're built for — students and early professionals figuring out financial independence for the first time — try one, abandon it within weeks, and go back to guessing.

A short survey we ran with this age group pointed to three recurring barriers, in order of how often they came up: forgetting to log expenses, the app feeling confusing to navigate, and the process simply taking too long. The result is a familiar pattern — overspending, losing track of day-to-day expenses, avoiding any kind of goal-based planning, and slowly giving up on the habit altogether.

The gap isn't financial literacy. It's that existing tools ask for more effort and attention than a beginner is willing to give.
02
Approach

Understanding the problem before designing for it.

Before proposing anything, the goal was to understand how young adults actually relate to money — their tracking habits, where existing tools fall short, and what the wider industry data says about this age group's financial behaviour.

Case studies

Looking at how other products and services have approached financial behaviour change for young, first-time earners.

Existing data

Pulling from published reports and studies on Gen Z spending, saving, and financial literacy patterns.

Market analysis

Reviewing the finance and budgeting tools already available, and where their design choices help or hurt adoption.

03
Findings

Six patterns kept surfacing across the research.

Each pattern below is backed by the original source clippings gathered during research — news pieces, industry reports, and first-person posts. Click any clipping to view it full-size.

＋

People want to manage money, but struggle to keep any tracking habit consistent.

＋

Gen Z spends more visibly than previous generations, but reports lower financial literacy.

＋

Finance apps have a retention problem — installs are high, continued use is not.

＋

Budgeting, as most apps frame it, creates stress, guilt, and negative emotion rather than confidence.

＋

Privacy and data security are a real hesitation, especially for anything linked to a bank account.

＋

Most tools are feature-heavy in ways that don’t line up with how people actually behave day to day.

Low retention

People download finance apps but stop using them over time, largely from a lack of engagement and habit support.

Logging friction

Manual entry and multi-step flows make people drop off, breaking the tracking routine before it forms.

Financial pressure

Current apps tend to create pressure and guilt, instead of making money management feel manageable.

Motivation matters

People need some sense of reward or progress to stay consistent with a financial habit over time.

Simple interface

A clean, minimal interface consistently outperforms a feature-heavy one for this audience.

04
Landscape review

Reading six existing tools against the same six questions.

To see where the gap actually was, we reviewed six widely-used budgeting and expense tools side by side — not for feature counts, but for where each one holds a beginner's attention, and where it loses it.

Tool Core strength Where it works well Where it falls short
Monefy Ultra-fast expense entry Great for quick, daily logging No insight or motivation loop — people drift away
Good Budget Structured budgeting system Good for planned allocation of money Too manual and time-consuming for daily use
Money Manager Feature-rich tracking and reports Strong analytics and customisation No automation — functional, but not engaging
Money Tracker All-in-one finance management Covers many needs in one place Feels cluttered, little guidance for beginners
Wallet Advanced automation, bank sync Powerful for detailed financial control Overwhelming for anyone new to budgeting
Spendee Visual, shared budgeting Good interface, group expense features Limited motivation or habit-building support

Speed vs. depth gap

People are pushed to choose between ease of use and real financial understanding — nothing reviewed balanced both.

Cognitive overload

Beginners need a guided experience, not a feature-heavy one — otherwise they disengage early.

High effort, quick drop-off

The moment tracking starts to feel like a task, people stop sustaining it. Low effort is what keeps a habit alive.

Low emotional engagement

Most tools treat money purely as data, when people respond far more to motivation and small emotional cues.

Money is social

Managing money isn't a purely private act — it's social too, and almost nothing reviewed supports that.

05
Primary research

Going straight to the people this is about.

Secondary research explains the industry. It doesn't tell you how one specific 19-year-old actually feels the night before rent is due. For that, we ran a two-part primary study: a branched survey, and a set of short interviews — both aimed at the same 18–25 age group.

Students & early college goers

Managing limited allowances or part-time income. Want to track daily spend and learn budgeting basics. Save for short-term goals — trips, festivals, gadgets. Prefer simple, visual interfaces and respond well to gamified rewards.

Young working professionals

Recently financially independent, learning to manage a salary. Want to balance spending and saving, and plan medium-term goals like rent or investing. Appreciate clean dashboards and habit tracking over gamification.

Method

Run entirely digitally, fitting a tech-savvy audience: a two-path Google Form (current users vs. non-users, 45 responses) and short personal interviews with 18 students and young adults.

Two very different research instruments — a form and a conversation — kept surfacing the same word: effort.

The survey

Branching the form into current users and non-users let us see both sides of the same habit: why people keep going, and why people quietly stop.

Behaviour & adoption

  • Most respondents are beginners — mostly aged 19–21, still in college
  • Most want to start budgeting but haven't yet
  • Current tracking habits are weak: mental tracking, notes, or Excel outnumber app use
  • Even when apps are used, it's inconsistent — weekly or monthly at best

Barriers, needs & preferences

  • Top barriers: too confusing, too time-consuming, forgetting to log, feels boring, trust and privacy concerns
  • What would help: easy setup, rewards and gamification, visual charts, and privacy reassurance
  • Strong preference for minimal, clean UI and automatic UPI/bank syncing

High effort

People don't avoid budgeting because they don't care — they avoid it because it feels like work.

Manual friction

If an app demands consistent manual input, people already know they won't keep it up.

Overwhelming finance

Current apps come across as serious, complex, and heavy — before a person even opens them.

Needs motivation

Rewards, gamification, and a sense of fun came up again and again.

Needs guidance

People want a tool that teaches and suggests — not just one that records.

The interviews

18 short conversations with students and young adults, focused on what they liked about finance apps, what frustrated them, and what made them stop using one. We organised what we heard using affinity mapping.

“I would like it if the app gives me warnings on spending or reminders to invest.”

“I have difficulty trusting an app to connect to my UPI account.”

“I love the calendar feature, so I can see which days I spent the least and most.”

＋

People want to track money but don't stay consistent over time.

＋

Many find finance apps too effort-heavy for daily use.

＋

Constantly monitoring spending brings on anxiety and guilt for a lot of people.

＋

Trust in connecting a bank or UPI account to a third-party app is low.

＋

People prefer quick, visual ways to understand spending — calendars, summaries — over raw numbers.

＋

Most only ever touch the basic features; advanced tools go ignored.

＋

Shared expenses — with friends, on trips, with roommates — are a consistent pain point.

＋

Existing apps don't support group expense tracking in any meaningful way.

＋

People bounce between several apps, or fall back to manual methods, depending on the need.

Consistency drops

Long-term habit formation is the core failure point, more than any single feature gap.

High effort

Effort — not disinterest — is the biggest reason people stop using a tool.

Negative emotions

Stress and guilt don't just accompany tracking, they actively push people away from it.

Trust barrier

Without trust in how an app handles bank access, adoption fails before it starts.

Social money

Real financial behaviour is shared — split bills, group trips — but apps largely ignore it.

Bringing it together

Every sticky note from the interviews and open survey responses went onto one board, then got grouped by hand into recurring themes.

Pain points

  • Current apps feel outdated, cluttered, hard to navigate
  • Too many ads, limited free features
  • Hard to track or re-categorise expenses
  • No easy way to review past spending
  • Privacy and trust issues throughout

Desired features

  • Better categorisation and organisation
  • Photo uploads of receipts with automatic reading
  • Budgeting guidance, not just tracking
  • Collaborative and group-split features
  • Daily limits, personalised insights, monthly recaps

Behaviour & motivation

  • Learns better visually, through graphs
  • Logs payments but forgets to categorise them
  • Gets bored easily; wants something simple and spontaneous
  • Wants reduced anxiety around money, not more of it
  • Responds to streaks, milestones, and gamified progress

Trust & social

  • Wants a friendly, informal tone — not a spreadsheet
  • Strong interest in group savings and split expenses
  • Concerned about privacy and security
  • Hesitant about UPI integration specifically
06
Synthesis

What the research pointed to.

Put together, the survey data, secondary research, and landscape review all pointed at the same underlying issue: the problem for this age group was never a lack of features. It was friction, tone, and the absence of any reason to come back tomorrow.

A useful financial tool for this audience has to reduce effort at every step, and give people a reason to feel good about showing up — not just a place to enter numbers.
